projects.detail: Optimization and AI-based decision support for strategic planning of humanitarian logistics operations.
projects.context: I contributed to a decision support system for planning humanitarian relief operations. The project combined mathematical optimization with a priority-based heuristic to select participating organizations, allocate supplies, and choose transport modes and delivery speeds. The model accounts for delivery priorities, available resources, and the costs of supplies, delays, fuel and crews.

The model weighs safety, economic and environmental benefits subject to budget and closure eligibility constraints. A selection heuristic and an interactive interface support comparisons of alternative closure strategies.

researchStatement: Operations research, mathematical optimization and artificial intelligence for logistics, industrial and service systems.
biography: I am a Postdoctoral Scholar at the University of Washington, Tacoma Campus. Before joining UW in June 2026, I was a Postdoctoral Research Scholar at Florida State University, where I earned my Ph.D. in Civil Engineering with a focus on operations research and logistics optimization. Dr. Maxim A. Dulebenets advised my dissertation. I also hold a Master of Engineering in Civil Engineering from Florida State University and a B.S. in Harbor, Waterway and Coastal Engineering from Wuhan University.

My research brings together operations research, mathematical optimization and artificial intelligence to study how logistics, industrial and service systems are designed and operated. I focus on operational planning, scheduling, resource allocation and disruption management, particularly when decisions at one facility or stage constrain what can be done elsewhere. My collaborators and I have used this perspective to develop compact formulations and decomposition algorithms for berth scheduling, and to combine adaptive search with exact optimization in truck scheduling. These studies illustrate a broader methodological interest in how the structure of a decision problem can guide both modeling and computation.

My published work spans maritime transportation, freight distribution, infrastructure safety and sustainable operations. It has appeared in Transportation Research Parts D and E, IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems, Swarm and Evolutionary Computation, and Reliability Engineering & System Safety. As a research assistant, I contributed to federally sponsored work on humanitarian relief logistics and to a Florida Department of Transportation study on highway–rail crossing closures. I have also helped develop research proposals, taught graduate courses as a teaching assistant, mentored undergraduate and master’s researchers, and reviewed for more than 20 peer-reviewed journals.

I am interested in how organizations can prepare for disruption through capacity, inventory and operating flexibility, and how they should revise plans as new information becomes available. In automated production and distribution, this means examining how investments in equipment change the constraints on daily operations. In healthcare and emergency response, I am interested in how local scheduling and allocation decisions affect access and continuity of service. Across these settings, I study where learning can improve a decision and how optimization can preserve the operating requirements that make it feasible.
homeResearch: I am interested in how strategic, tactical and operational decisions should be connected. System design and investment determine the capacity available for daily operations; schedules and allocation policies determine how effectively that capacity serves demand. My research examines these relationships within facilities, across networks and among organizations with different objectives. Coordination, uncertainty and the distribution of operating benefits and risks are central questions.

My methodological research concerns mathematical representations and computational methods for constrained decisions. Published studies develop compact mixed-integer formulations, decomposition approaches and adaptive hyperheuristics. Developing interests include reinforcement learning, generative and agentic AI, and quantum-assisted optimization. I am interested in how these approaches can support model formulation, algorithm design and sequential decisions, and when their contribution improves the complete decision process.

Maritime transportation, logistics and supply chains provide important applications, including berth and terminal operations, liner-shipping recovery and coordination of production, inventory and distribution. My interests also extend to manufacturing and automated operations, healthcare and laboratory scheduling, humanitarian logistics and emergency response. These settings share questions about resource dependencies and service, while introducing different operational requirements and priorities.

My longer-term agenda links resilient and sustainable system design with technology adoption and adaptive operations. I am interested in how preparedness affects recovery, how electrification and automation change bottlenecks, and how information sharing and decision authority influence coordination. Broader goals include understanding when investment, organizational arrangements or better operating policies offer the most effective improvement.
academicContext: I earned my Ph.D. in Civil Engineering from Florida State University in August 2025 under the supervision of Dr. Maxim A. Dulebenets. Florida State University also awarded me a Master of Engineering in Civil Engineering in December 2024 during my doctoral studies. I received my Bachelor of Science in Harbor, Waterway and Coastal Engineering from Wuhan University in June 2022.

My dissertation developed adaptive hyperheuristics for berth scheduling at marine container terminals. During my graduate and postdoctoral appointments at Florida State University, I also worked on mathematical formulations and solution methods for freight distribution and on sponsored research in humanitarian logistics and transportation infrastructure.

I held a postdoctoral appointment at Florida State University from August 2025 through May 2026. At the University of Washington, Tacoma Campus, I have worked with Dr. Angela Kitali on transportation research and proposals involving computer vision and geospatial data for infrastructure inventories.

homeQuestions: How should system design, investment and operational decisions be coordinated across resources, organizations and time scales?
How can optimization, learning and emerging computational methods support decisions under uncertainty and changing information?
How do preparedness, technological change and the organization of decisions affect resilience, sustainability and service performance?

collaborationProfiles.title: Mathematical optimization and logistics
collaborationProfiles.people: Dr. Maxim A. Dulebenets and collaborators
collaborationProfiles.text: My doctoral and postdoctoral research with Dr. Maxim A. Dulebenets developed formulations and algorithms for berth scheduling and cross-docking. This collaboration examines how compact models, decomposition and adaptive search can exploit operational structure, with published studies addressing both the design of solution methods and their computational performance.
collaborationProfiles.label: Compact models and decomposition

collaborationProfiles.title: Port electrification and transportation infrastructure
collaborationProfiles.people: Dr. Angela Kitali, Soud Mbegele and project collaborators
collaborationProfiles.text: My published work with Soud Mbegele and Dr. Angela Kitali examines how the Northwest Seaport Alliance translated shore power commitments into implementation responsibilities. I also contribute to research planning on computer vision and geospatial analysis for transportation facility inventories.
collaborationProfiles.label: Shore power commitments and implementation accountability

collaborationProfiles.title: Safety and resource allocation
collaborationProfiles.people: Dr. Ren Moses, Dr. Eren E. Ozguven, Dr. John Sobanjo and research coauthors
collaborationProfiles.text: Our joint work uses mathematical optimization to prioritize highway–rail crossing closures and allocate safety investments. The linked study considers safety, economic and environmental outcomes. Related work compares closure, countermeasure installation and grade separation under budget and eligibility constraints.
collaborationProfiles.label: Rail-crossing decision study

collaborationProfiles.title: Adaptive algorithms and sustainable systems
collaborationProfiles.people: Dr. Marta Borowska-Stefańska, Dr. Szymon Wiśniewski, Dr. Yui-Yip Lau and research coauthors
collaborationProfiles.text: These collaborations include berth-scheduling reviews, adaptive cross-docking algorithms, ship-schedule recovery and studies of electric-vehicle and tugboat operations. They combine mathematical modeling with different forms of evidence, including computational comparison, literature synthesis and industry interviews. The common methodological interest is how operating constraints and competing objectives should shape the model and its solution procedure.

homeResearchBrief: I study how to coordinate decisions across facilities, organizations and time horizons. The research below covers three connected questions: how to formulate and solve coupled decisions, how to coordinate operations across a system, and how to protect service as conditions change.
